A few words to know

unsuccessful applicant
Someone who applied but was not selected.
independent

communicate
To make information known to someone.
decision notice

consistently

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's latest email arrived with an attachment rather than another cautious description. The records team had located a printed sheet setting out the 2011 student travel scheme's review procedure. Because the sheet contained no personal information, Fiona was able to send Emma a copy. The folder labelled Appeals and reviews, however, remained unopened.

Emma read the document with the September newspaper cuttings beside her. According to the procedure, an unsuccessful applicant could request a review in writing within fourteen days of receiving a decision. The review was supposed to be handled by someone who had not taken part in the original selection.

That was a more useful detail than the folder's title, but it raised questions of its own. No reviewer was named on the sheet, and it did not explain how an independent person was appointed. Emma noted the difference between a written rule and evidence that the rule had been followed.

“Then an appeal was possible,” Sarah said when Emma called.

“On paper. We have no appeal letters, no completed reviews and no evidence that anyone was told how to request one.”

“Could the parent who wrote to the newspaper have appealed?”

“Perhaps. But a letter to an editor isn't the same as a formal request to the trust.”

Emma examined the parent's published complaint again. It questioned the lack of clear information about selection. It did not identify an application, describe a decision notice or mention a review request. Emma added a separate heading to her notes: Communication of the rules. A procedure could exist without being clearly explained to the people entitled to use it.

She returned to the original newspaper announcement of eight selected students and the later correction. Neither item gave the true selection total. The newly discovered sheet could not repair that gap: it concerned what happened after an unsuccessful decision, not the number of decisions made. Nor did it establish whether any grant had been paid.

Fiona telephoned that afternoon. The records team had identified several folders in the storage box but needed to check their condition and contents before describing them more precisely. No one had yet opened the folder about appeals. Fiona agreed to ask whether the trust held a record of reviewers or evidence that applicants had received the procedure.

Emma thanked her without pressing for names. She did not need a former student's identity to establish whether rules had been communicated consistently.

Later, she checked the date at the bottom of the procedure: August 2011. It therefore predated both the public announcement and Claire's disappearance. That made it relevant to the historical process, although a dated document did not prove it had reached every applicant.

Sarah texted: Can we say students had a right to appeal?

Emma considered the wording before replying: The written scheme offered a review. We can't yet say who knew about it or whether it was used.

For the next stage, she wrote one question in the margin: Where was this procedure given to applicants?
